title: Multithreading and Concurrency
goal: Threads, race conditions, synchronization, executors aur CompletableFuture.
objectives: Create threads with Runnable and run work on an ExecutorService
Explain a race condition and fix it with the right primitive
Use CompletableFuture to compose asynchronous steps
Recognise deadlock and avoid shared mutable state
definition: A thread is an independent path of execution inside one process, sharing that process's heap. Concurrency is managing multiple threads safely: without coordination, interleaved reads and writes cause race conditions. Java provides synchronized, volatile, atomics, locks, concurrent collections and executors for this.
explain: Every Java program starts with the main thread. You create another by implementing Runnable and passing it to a Thread, but production code submits tasks to an ExecutorService so threads are pooled and reused instead of created per request.

A race condition happens when two threads read-modify-write the same variable and the interleaving loses an update. count++ is three steps, not one. synchronized makes a block atomic and establishes visibility; AtomicInteger uses a compare-and-set loop; volatile only guarantees visibility, not atomicity of compound actions.

Deadlock happens when threads wait on locks in opposite orders forever. Prevent it by locking in one global order, keeping critical sections small, using timeouts (tryLock) and avoiding nested locks. CompletableFuture composes asynchronous work without blocking a thread on every step; virtual threads (Java 21) make blocking code cheap, but they are an implementation option, not a replacement for understanding shared state.
hinglish: Program main thread se shuru hota hai. Naya kaam Thread + Runnable se ho sakta hai, par production me ExecutorService use karte hain taaki threads pool se reuse hon. count++ teen steps hai, isliye do threads beech me ghus kar update kho sakte hain — yahi race condition hai.

synchronized block ko atomic banata hai aur visibility deta hai; AtomicInteger compare-and-set use karta hai; volatile sirf visibility deta hai, compound action atomic nahi karta. Deadlock tab hota hai jab threads ulte order me locks maangte hain — lock order fix karo, critical section chhota rakho.
analogy: Ek process ek kitchen hai aur threads usme kaam karne wale cooks. Shared counter fridge par laga board hai: do cooks ek saath padhein, dono +1 likhein, to ek update kho jaata hai. synchronized ka matlab hai board par ek waqt me ek hi cook likhega.
why: Servers handle many requests at once, and concurrency bugs are the hardest to reproduce. Interviews ask about thread lifecycle, synchronized vs volatile, executors and CompletableFuture because those are the tools every Java backend uses daily.

syntax.note: start() creates the new path of execution; run() would run it on the current thread. join() makes the caller wait.
submit returns a Future for the result; always shut the pool down or the JVM may keep running.

topics.title: Process vs thread
topics.body: A process has its own memory; threads share the process heap but have their own stack and program counter. Sharing makes communication cheap and race conditions possible.

topics.title: Thread lifecycle and creation
topics.body: NEW → RUNNABLE → (BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING) → TERMINATED. Create with Runnable (preferred) or by extending Thread. start() schedules; run() is just a method call.

topics.title: ExecutorService and thread pools
topics.body: Pools bound the number of threads and reuse them. submit returns Future; invokeAll runs a batch. shutdown lets queued work finish, shutdownNow interrupts. Never create a thread per request in a server.

topics.title: Synchronization and race conditions
topics.body: synchronized(lock) makes a block mutually exclusive and publishes writes. Use one lock object consistently. Keep the critical section small; never call unknown code (or I/O) while holding a lock.

topics.title: volatile, atomics and locks
topics.body: volatile guarantees visibility of a single variable but not atomicity. AtomicInteger/AtomicLong/LongAdder handle counters lock-free. ReentrantLock adds tryLock timeouts and fairness. Prefer the simplest tool that is correct.

topics.title: wait/notify and concurrent collections
topics.body: wait/notify coordinate on an object's monitor but are easy to misuse; prefer BlockingQueue for producer-consumer. ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList and BlockingQueue are the thread-safe collections.

topics.title: CompletableFuture and deadlock
topics.body: CompletableFuture composes async steps with thenApply/thenCompose/thenCombine and handles errors with exceptionally. Deadlock: two threads hold one lock each and wait for the other — fix the lock order or use timeouts.

topics.title: Virtual threads (Java 21)
topics.body: Virtual threads are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM, so blocking code can scale to many tasks. They reduce the cost of thread-per-task designs; they do not make shared mutable state safe.

examples.title: Two threads, one safe counter
lines: Both threads share one Counter object, so they share the counter state.
increment is synchronized, so the read-modify-write cannot interleave.
join makes main wait for both workers before reading the total.
dryRun: thread a and b each loop 1000 times
each increment is atomic under the monitor

examples.title: ExecutorService and futures
lines: A fixed pool of two threads runs three tasks, reusing threads.
invokeAll submits every callable and returns futures in the same order.
get() blocks until that task's result is available.

mistakes.wrong: private int count; void inc() { count++; }
mistakes.right: private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(); void inc() { count.incrementAndGet(); }
mistakes.why: count++ is not atomic; two threads can read the same value and lose an update. Use atomics or synchronize the whole operation.

mistakes.wrong: synchronized (a) { synchronized (b) { … } }  // other thread locks b then a
mistakes.right: Always acquire locks in the same global order, or use one lock.
mistakes.why: Opposite lock orders are the classic deadlock recipe.

debug.brief: This program throws IllegalThreadStateException because it starts the same thread twice. Fix it.
hints: A Thread can be started only once.
Create a new thread for the second run, or start it once.

best: Prefer executors and concurrent collections over raw threads and wait/notify.
Keep shared mutable state minimal; immutable objects need no locks.
Never call blocking I/O or unknown code while holding a lock.
Use timeouts and a consistent lock order to make deadlock unlikely and detectable.
tip: For 'synchronized vs volatile', say synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility, volatile gives visibility only. Then give the counter example: volatile count++ is still broken.
revision: Threads share the heap; each has its own stack.
Race condition = interleaved read-modify-write; fix with synchronization or atomics.
Executors pool threads; Futures return results.
CompletableFuture composes async steps; virtual threads make blocking cheap.

practice.title: Thread-safe counter
practice.prompt: Run four threads incrementing an AtomicInteger 1000 times each and print the total.
practice.hint: Join every thread before reading the value.

practice.title: Producer-consumer
practice.prompt: Use a BlockingQueue with one producer and one consumer; print consumed items in order.

practice.title: Async chain
practice.prompt: Use CompletableFuture.supplyAsync to double a number, then thenApply to add 1, and print the result.
practice.hint: join() waits for the final stage.

mcqs.explain: Only one thread executes the block at a time, and writes are visible to the next holder.

mcqs.q: Which is safe for a shared counter?
mcqs.explain: AtomicInteger performs the increment as one atomic operation.

options: Threads waiting on locks held by each other in a cycle
mcqs.explain: A circular wait on locks is the classic cause.

interview.a: volatile makes reads and writes of one variable visible across threads and prevents reordering, but a compound action like count++ is still unsafe. synchronized provides mutual exclusion plus visibility, so it protects multi-step invariants.
interview.followUp: When is volatile enough? (A single-writer status flag or a reference published once, where no compound update is needed.)

interview.a: Acquire locks in a global order, avoid nested locks, keep critical sections small, use tryLock with a timeout, and prefer lock-free structures or a single lock when contention is low.
interview.followUp: Can you recover from a deadlock? (Not reliably; you can detect it with thread dumps and restart, which is why prevention matters.)

lab.title: Thread-safe total

hints: Use AtomicInteger or a synchronized block around count++.
